title: i3 Threat Advisory: Identifying North Korean IT Workers — Email IOCs Appendix
description: A bulk list of email addresses DTEX's i3 threat intelligence team has observed associated with DPRK IT-worker operations, published as a public appendix so defenders can cross-check their own HR/recruitment records. Compiled by DTEX from third-party reporting connected to observed IT-worker operations.
disclaimer: Per DTEX's own advisory text: these IOCs are NOT indicative of a confirmed North-Korea-attributed hack — they may have associations with IT-worker operations and require further investigation if observed in your environment. Any connection to actual persons may be deliberate (an operator using a real person's identity) or incidental, and the actual owner of an email account listed here may be unaware their address is associated with this IOC list. Do not treat presence on this list as proof of wrongdoing by the account holder.

source.title: i3 Threat Advisory: Identifying North Korean IT Workers: Key Threat Indicators

excluded_notes: 3 decoded value(s) from the source did not match a valid email format (e.g. a stray numeric suffix like '-13' appended in the source's own table cell) and were excluded rather than guessed at.

title: US v. Virtual Currency Associated with North Korean IT Worker Money Laundering: seized addresses
description: Unhosted virtual-currency addresses seized under warrants 22-sz-6, 22-sz-13, 22-sz-18 and 22-sz-19, together with addresses whose stablecoin balances the issuer froze at law enforcement's request. Taken from Attachment A rather than from the body of the complaint: the body also names addresses in its narrative that are not part of the seized property, and the attachment is the bounded list the filing itself describes as complete.
disclaimer: These are the addresses named in a civil forfeiture complaint as property the United States seized or had frozen, drawn from the complaint's Attachment A, which the filing introduces as listing in full every unhosted wallet address from which law enforcement seized funds in this investigation. A forfeiture complaint is an allegation against property rather than a conviction of any person: it states the government's case for why the funds are forfeitable, and the case had not been decided when this was recorded. Presence here says an address was seized or frozen in this action, not that any particular person has been found to have done anything.

source.title: Verified Complaint for Forfeiture in Rem, United States v. Virtual Currency Associated with North Korean IT Worker Money Laundering and Sanctions Evasion Conspiracies, No. 1:25-cv-01769 (D.D.C.)
source.publisher: U.S. Department of Justice, U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia

excluded_notes: Three addresses appear in the complaint narrative but not in Attachment A, and are not carried by this dataset, whose bound is the attachment. One of the three is nonetheless indexed, independently, from the scraper reading the complaint prose and quoting the sentence that names it; that is a separate provenance path with its own context rather than a contradiction of this bound. Entries are stored lowercased to match what the wallet normalizer emits, so a dataset entry and a scraped match of the same address resolve to one record instead of two.

title: PolinRider npm, Go and PHP compromises: command-and-control addresses
description: Addresses the report's indicator table gives for this wave: a primary command-and-control host, a stage-two loader, and two further hosts it says are shared with infrastructure already attributed to PolinRider.
disclaimer: Third-party-reported, not independently verified by Chollima Hunter. The report marks two of these as novel to the incident it describes and the rest as already shared with PolinRider infrastructure, which is why most were already held here from other reporting; carrying them again records the corroboration rather than adding new claims. These are the attacker-side entries from the report's indicator table only. The 27 compromised packages and Go modules it also lists are the projects that were attacked, and naming those as indicators would name the victims.

title: Astrill VPN exit addresses published by Spur
description: IPv4 addresses Spur attributes to the Astrill VPN service, released free in December 2024 alongside its post on the service's use in DPRK remote-worker fraud. Spur, whose business is attributing anonymising infrastructure, published about 2,400 addresses it recorded as active on 19 December 2024 and said its customers were continuing to report fraudulent remote-worker applications arriving from them.
disclaimer: These are the exit addresses of a commercial VPN service with customers everywhere. An address on this list says that a connection came through Astrill, which DPRK IT workers are documented to favour; it does not say who was behind the connection, and the great majority of traffic through these exits is ordinary customers. Treat a match as a reason to look at the account behind it, not as evidence about the person. The list is a snapshot of the addresses active on 19 December 2024; VPN exits are reassigned over time, so an address here may since have been returned to its hosting provider and given to someone else. The list is Spur's and is carried here as published.

source.title: Astrill VPN and DPRK Remote Worker Fraud

excluded_notes: 7 line(s) in the source were not a single routable IPv4 host address (a .0 network address, a reserved range, or not an address at all) and were excluded rather than guessed at.

title: Free proxy servers listed by IPRoyal
description: IPv4 addresses of the free, public proxy servers IPRoyal lists on its site, as read on the sync date. Reporting on DPRK remote-worker cases in 2026 names IPRoyal beside Astrill VPN as a service the workers route through; carrying the public list lets a defender label a connection that came through one of these proxies.
disclaimer: This is IPRoyal's directory of free public proxies, not the company's paid residential network, and the servers on it belong to third parties and are used by anyone who finds the list. A match says that a connection came through a public proxy that IPRoyal listed on the day the list was read; it says nothing about who was behind it. Free proxies rotate within days, so the list is a snapshot that the weekly sync replaces, and an address here may since have gone back to ordinary use. Treat a match as a reason to look at the account behind it, never as evidence about the person.
excluded_notes: 728 record(s) on the list were excluded because the index does not carry the address: CDN edge addresses (most of them Cloudflare's, shared by millions of sites), network or reserved addresses, public resolvers, or a value that is not a dotted IPv4 address with a valid port.
